title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
For as long as humans have existed, innovations and discoveries have changed the way we live. We learnt to shelter in caves, discovered fire, learnt to make it ourselves, and used it to forge tools and shape the things we needed to survive. Each of these steps altered what it meant to be human.
Before going further, I want to point out something hidden beneath all of this. The moment we learn how to do something properly, it becomes autonomous. Our body takes over, and the brain only steps in at critical moments. Think about walking. As children, we have to learn it step by step, but once we master it, we never notice how we walk again. The brain simply decides where we need to go, and the body follows.
Try this: can you explain exactly how you stand up from a chair? Probably not, at least not until you actually do it, slowly, and watch yourself. That is the point. Once something becomes routine, it runs on its own, without needing our conscious attention.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
section: From the Wheel to the Horse
text:
From the Wheel to the Horse
Keep that idea in mind, because it repeats throughout history: every major innovation either takes over a routine skill, or turns a new skill into one we no longer think about.
The wheel is one of the earliest examples. It appeared in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE, first as the potter’s wheel and soon after on carts. Before it, moving anything heavy meant carrying it, dragging it, or rolling it on logs, and each of those took constant, deliberate effort. The wheel did not make people stronger. It made strength matter less, and the attention it freed went into other things.
Riding animals followed the same pattern, but inside the human body. Learning to ride a horse is hard. You have to balance, read the animal, and coordinate your legs, hands, and weight all at once. Yet once a rider masters it, riding becomes like walking: the rider decides where to go, and the body handles how. A skilled rider can scan the horizon, talk, or plan the day while the riding happens underneath. One skill became autonomous, and in doing so it extended how far a person could go.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
Driving Into a Bigger World
Then came engines and the car, and the same story played out on a much larger scale.
For most of history, a person’s world was the region they could walk or ride across. A journey between countries took weeks or months, and travelling around the world was something almost no one would do in a lifetime. Engines changed that. Cars, trains, ships, and later aeroplanes shrank the planet. Today you can cross a continent in an afternoon, circle the globe in a couple of days, and people have even left the planet entirely and travelled to space.
Driving itself followed the walking pattern. Every new driver remembers how overwhelming the first lesson was: mirrors, pedals, gears, signals, and the road all at once. A few months later, most drivers arrive home with little memory of the journey. The driving became autonomous, and the conscious mind returned to the only thing that really needed it: deciding where to go, and reacting when something unexpected happens.

We always resist first
What I find most striking is not the technology itself but how people reacted to it. Almost every one of these innovations was resisted at first, and later embraced so completely that we cannot imagine living without it.
When the first self-propelled road vehicles appeared in Britain, the Locomotive Act of 1865, better known as the “Red Flag Act”, required a person to walk in front of them, carrying a red flag to warn others. A machine capable of going faster than walking pace was legally slowed down to the speed of a pedestrian. The rule was not fully lifted until 1896.
Many people simply refused to give up their horses. Early motorists were often mocked with the shout “Get a horse!”, and for years horses and cars shared the same streets. Yet within a few decades the horse had all but disappeared from everyday transport. People did not switch because someone convinced them in an argument. They switched because the car was better, and the world reorganised itself around it.
We are watching the same story play out again today with electric cars. Just as petrol cars were once the future of transport, electric cars are the future now, and just as people once insisted on keeping their horses, many today insist on keeping their petrol cars. There is a nice irony here: around 1900, electric cars were a serious contender on the roads before petrol engines won the first round. They are now coming back, and I believe they will eventually dominate the market as completely as the car replaced the horse.
The pattern is much older than cars. In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates argues that writing would weaken people’s memory, because they would rely on marks on a page instead of remembering things themselves. In the early nineteenth century, the Luddites smashed the textile machines they feared would destroy their livelihoods. Every time, the fear was not entirely wrong: something real was lost. But every time, what was gained turned out to be far larger, and the next generation could not see what the fuss had been about.
So what finally breaks the resistance? Usually, the new technology simply proves itself over time, as the car did. But sometimes, all it needs is a shock. For decades, x86 processors ruled personal computers and servers, and anything else was treated as a joke outside phones and embedded devices. Then, in 2020, Apple put its Arm-based M1 chip into serious machines like the MacBook Air and the Mac mini, and it shocked the industry. It was faster, cooler, and far more efficient than the x86 chips it replaced. Within a few years, Arm was everywhere that had once belonged to x86: laptops, cloud servers, and even supercomputers. And Apple’s unified memory, where the CPU and GPU share a single fast pool of memory, went from an unusual design choice to a feature that every competitor now rushes to copy to stay relevant. Arm had been capable for years. It took one company willing to take the risk and show the world that it was equal, or even superior. Maybe RISC-V is next, waiting for its own M1 moment. But I am drifting off topic now.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
The Calculator and the Human “Computers”
The example closest to AI, in my opinion, is the calculator.
Before electronic machines, “computer” was a job title. Rooms full of people, many of them women, and many highly trained in mathematics, performed calculations by hand for astronomy, engineering, ballistics, and aeronautics. Entire industries depended on human arithmetic.
Calculating machines took that job away. And the early ones were not even fully reliable. Mechanical calculators going back to Pascal and Leibniz in the seventeenth century had trouble with carrying digits correctly, and some of the early pocket electronic calculators of the 1970s gave noticeably inaccurate results for functions like logarithms and trigonometry. It took years of engineering before people could simply trust whatever number appeared on the screen. Today nobody double-checks a calculator, we assume it is right, and we are almost always correct to.
That history is worth remembering whenever someone dismisses AI because it still makes mistakes. Reliability is something technologies earn over time. It is rarely there on day one.
So what happened to the human computers? Many of those jobs disappeared, but they were replaced by something better. At NACA (later NASA), Dorothy Vaughan, who led a unit of human computers, saw that electronic computers were coming for her team’s work. Instead of fighting it, she taught herself and her colleagues the programming language FORTRAN, and they became some of the agency’s early programmers. The boring arithmetic went to the machine, and the people moved up to more important work.
Mathematics as a whole followed the same path. Freed from grinding through calculations by hand, mathematicians and engineers could tackle problems that would have been impossible before: numerical simulation, statistics on huge datasets, and eventually the very machine learning that powers today’s AI. The calculator did not shrink the need for mathematics. It made the demand for it grow.

The pattern keeps repeating
Once you see this pattern, you find it everywhere:

GPS took over the work of reading maps and memorising routes. We now go to unfamiliar cities without a second thought and spend our attention on why we are going, not on how to get there.
Search engines changed what it means to know something. We no longer need to memorise every fact; we need to know what to ask and how to judge the answer.
Spell checkers and autocomplete handle the mechanics of writing, so the writer can focus on the argument.
Compilers freed programmers from writing machine code by hand, and an entire software industry was built on the time that saved.

In each case, a low-level skill was handed over to a machine, and the people involved moved up a level.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
How Something Becomes Autonomous
So how does a skill become autonomous in the first place? I think it happens in four stages:

We learn. Everything is deliberate, slow, and exhausting. Each step needs our full attention.
We master it. The skill becomes smooth, and the steps blend into a single fluid action.
We become observers. With the doing handled, our attention shifts outwards, to the environment and what is changing in it.
We decide. The world is not deterministic. When the environment looks familiar, we act automatically, exactly as before. When something changes, for example a child steps into the road, the ground is icy, or the horse is nervous, our observation pulls the brain back in, and we make a new decision.

Neuroscience describes something very similar. Researchers distinguish between habitual control, which is fast, cheap, and automatic, and goal-directed control, which is slow, deliberate, and flexible. The brain switches between them depending on how certain it is about the situation (Daw, Niv & Dayan, 2005). Routine situations run on habit, and surprises bring back deliberate thought.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
We Are Agents, Too
If this sounds familiar to anyone working in AI, it should: it is a description of an agent.
In reinforcement learning, an agent observes the state of its environment, takes actions according to a policy, and receives rewards, while trying to maximise its reward over time. Today’s agentic AI systems work in the same way. They observe, plan, act, and adjust when the world does not behave as expected.
Humans are agents in exactly this sense. We observe the world, act on it, and are rewarded or punished by the results. And our long history of handing skills over to tools is what a good agent does: it delegates routine work to cheap, reliable subroutines, so that its limited attention goes into the decisions that actually affect its reward.
Seen this way, AI is not a rival agent competing for our place. It is the next layer of autonomy in our own stack, after the body that walks, the horse that carries, the engine that drives, and the calculator that computes. AI takes on the routine cognitive work, such as drafting, searching, summarising, and writing boilerplate code, and leaves us the higher-level role: setting goals, noticing when something has changed, and making the decisions that matter.

Fighting the tide does not maximise reward
There is also a game-theory argument here. Imagine two people, two companies, or two countries, where one adopts a powerful new technology and the other refuses it. The refusing side does not stop the technology from existing. It just falls behind whoever adopts it. Whatever the other side chooses, refusing leaves you worse off. In game-theory terms, refusing is a dominated strategy.
Reinforcement learning makes the same point from another angle. An agent in a non-stationary environment, one whose rules change over time, cannot keep following the policy that worked yesterday. If it does, its reward steadily falls. Our environment is exactly this kind: every major innovation rewrites the rules. The rider who refused to learn to drive, or the computer who refused to learn FORTRAN, was following an outdated policy in a changed world.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
section: AI Is the Hand, We Are the Brain
text:
AI Is the Hand, We Are the Brain
Which brings us to AI.
Everything above has been building up to this point. The wheel took over carrying, the horse and then the engine took over travelling, and the calculator took over arithmetic. AI is next in line, and it is the broadest step yet. Any job that can be automated, or done autonomously, AI is going to take over. That includes writing routine code, filling in forms, summarising documents, sorting data, answering standard questions, and running the same analysis for the hundredth time. These are the cognitive equivalent of walking: tasks we once had to learn deliberately, and which no longer need our full attention once mastered.
This is not something to fear. It is the same division of labour our own bodies already use. When you walk, your legs do the walking and your brain decides where to go. It only steps in when something changes: a curb, a crowd, a slippery floor. AI gives us that same arrangement for our work. AI will be the hand, and humans will be the brain. AI does the doing; we observe and decide. We set the goals, watch the environment, notice when something is not right, and make the calls that require judgement, responsibility, and an understanding of what actually matters.
That is exactly the four-stage path from earlier, applied to a whole civilisation. We are moving past the learning and mastering stages for a huge range of tasks and into the stages that were always the most valuable: observing and deciding.

Walking against progress
Not everyone will accept this, just as not everyone accepted the car or the calculator. Some will insist on doing by hand what a machine can now do better and faster, and they will treat that as a virtue. But history is clear about how this ends. The person waving the red flag in front of the car did not stop the car. The human computer who refused to learn programming did not stop the computer. They only made sure that progress went on without them.
Anyone who fights against AI handling the low-level work is walking against progress, and, like the agent following an outdated policy, they will watch their reward fall while the world moves on.

title: Letting Go of the Wheel: Why I Am on AI’s Side
text:
Finding the Next Skill
So where does that leave us?
Not in a world without work, but in one where the work keeps moving up. Each innovation makes some skills obsolete and creates demand for new ones. Few people need to shoe a horse, do long division by hand, or read a paper map today, and almost nobody misses those jobs. In their place came skills nobody could have imagined before: driving, programming, data analysis, and now, directing and supervising AI systems.
The lesson I take from history is simple. Instead of holding on to skills that innovation has made obsolete, we should be looking for the new ones that it has created. We need to learn them, master them, let them become automatic, and then move up again. Let AI be the hand. Our job is to become a better brain: to observe more carefully, decide more wisely, and keep moving up. That is how we have always adapted, and I believe it is how we will build a better life alongside AI.

text:
Teaching a computer from examples



We give the computer examples: inputs and the correct answers
It tunes a flexible formula until its predictions match those answers
“Learning” means finding the parameters with the smallest error


You already do this: fit a curve to two or three experimental points, then predict other amounts of reactant without running more experiments.





C. M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer (2006), ch. 1.


Can we trust that curve everywhere, even far from the points we measured?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Inside the data versus outside it
text:
Inside the data versus outside it



Between known points the model interpolates, and is usually reliable
Beyond them it extrapolates, and nothing in the training checks it
Models that agree inside the data can disagree wildly outside it


A small training error says little about data the model has never seen.





C. M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer (2006), §1.1, §3.2.


Let’s see how different our interpretation of a molecule is from a computer’s.

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: What does a molecule look like to a computer?
text:
What does a molecule look like to a computer?



Input: each atom’s element and 3D position, exactly what an .xyz file holds
Output: the energy E, and the force on every atom
There are many ways to give a molecule to a computer: 3D coordinates, adjacency matrices, molecular graphs, SMILES strings, fingerprints


The model never sees a label like “carbonyl”: only elements and distances.





J. Behler, M. Parrinello, Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 146401 (2007); I. Batatia et al., NeurIPS (2022).


For ML people: these are equivariant graph neural networks (NequIP, MACE, EquiFormerV2). For chemists: the symmetry is built in, not learned.


Then does machine learning read molecules the way a chemist does?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Does machine learning read molecules this way?
text:
Does machine learning read molecules this way?



The model learns from whole molecules, one geometry at a time
Nothing forces it to learn “parts” the way a chemist does
It might learn rules, or it might memorise the molecules it was shown


If every part of a new molecule is familiar, does the model find the whole familiar?





B. Lake, M. Baroni, ICML (2018).


Where to get these data, and how?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Any method can supply the data and become a teacher
text:
Any method can supply the data and become a teacher



From CCSD(T) to GFN2-xTB, every method gives energies and forces for a geometry
So any of them can supply training data
Datasets range from ten small molecules (MD17) to over 100 million calculations (OMol25)


A model is at best as accurate as the method that produced its data.





S. Chmiela et al., Sci. Adv. 3, e1603015 (2017); C. Bannwarth, S. Ehlert, S. Grimme, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 15, 1652 (2019); D. S. Levine et al., arXiv (2025).


For ML people: this is a ladder of label quality versus label cost.


If these methods already give us energies and forces, why not just keep using them?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Why we invented semi-empirical methods



Cost grows steeply with size: roughly N4 for Hartree–Fock, N5 for MP2, N7 for CCSD(T)
Molecular dynamics needs energies and forces at millions of time steps
Semi-empirical methods replaced expensive integrals with fitted parameters


Every step down the ladder makes the same trade: accuracy for time and computer resources.





M. J. S. Dewar, W. Thiel, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 99, 4899 (1977); W. Thiel, WIREs Comput. Mol. Sci. 4, 145 (2014).


Machine learning makes a similar trade, by fitting to data. So what kind of method is it?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Enter machine-learning potentials



Learn from reference calculations once
Then predict energies and forces in milliseconds, close to the reference accuracy
Nanosecond MD at near-reference accuracy becomes routine


Is machine learning a numerical, a semi-empirical, or an empirical method?





J. Behler, Chem. Rev. 121, 10037 (2021).


Don’t answer the question. Pause and let both halves of the room think.


Whatever it is, it learns from data. If labels are this expensive, why not pay once, at scale, for all of chemistry?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Foundation models for atoms



More DFT calculations, bigger datasets: MPtrj (materials), OMol25 (molecules, 100M+ calculations)
Pre-train once on millions of structures, then fine-tune or use zero-shot
Examples: MACE-MP-0, UMA, PET-MAD


The assumption: they learn chemistry itself. Or do they stay grounded in what they have seen?





I. Batatia et al., arXiv:2401.00096 (2023); D. S. Levine et al., arXiv (2025); A. Mazitov et al., arXiv (2025).


Even with millions of structures, what happens where the data runs out?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
What the data covers



A model is only checked where its training data are
Room-temperature MD samples the energy well densely, and the steep repulsive wall almost never
On the wall the model has to guess, and it guesses wrong


High-energy geometries the data does not cover: one kind of out-of-distribution.





J. Behler, Chem. Rev. 121, 10037 (2021); X. Fu et al., Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (2023).


Now think of a reaction. Which point on the path does MD visit least?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Reactions: the rarest point matters most
text:
Reactions: the rarest point matters most



MD spends almost all its time in the reactant and product wells
The transition state is visited rarely, so it is barely in the data
At 298 K, every 1.4 kcal/mol of barrier error is a factor of 10 in the rate


Rare events the data barely covers: a second kind of out-of-distribution.





H. Eyring, J. Chem. Phys. 3, 107 (1935).


From k ∝ exp(−ΔG‡/RT): RT ln 10 ≈ 1.36 kcal/mol at 298 K. Schematic profile.


Steep walls, rare events… what else counts as out-of-distribution?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Many ways to be out-of-distribution


Out-of-distribution: anything the training data does not represent, where the model has to go beyond its data rather than fill in between it.

High-energy geometries; rare events
Higher temperature than in training
Elements, charges or spin states never seen
Solvent or surfaces, when trained in vacuum
A new combination of known groups





S. Chmiela et al., Sci. Adv. 3, e1603015 (2017); X. Fu et al., Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (2023).


All but the last change the conditions. The last one changes only the composition: every part is covered, the whole is not.


Which of these do we actually test when we evaluate ML potentials today?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: How ML potentials are evaluated today
text:
How ML potentials are evaluated today


Random splits
Test frames come from the same MD trajectories as training frames, so they are near-copies of what the model saw
Shifts in conditions
Higher temperature, distorted geometries, rare events, unseen elements

Scaffold splits
Standard for predicting molecular properties (MoleculeNet), but not used for potentials
What is missing
A controlled shift in composition: every part seen, only the whole new


The test chemists would care about most, a new molecule built from known groups, is the one we rarely run.


S. Chmiela et al., Sci. Adv. 3, e1603015 (2017); X. Fu et al., TMLR (2023); Z. Wu et al., Chem. Sci. 9, 513 (2018).


Shouldn’t these models handle new combinations anyway? After all, they are built from local parts.

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Locality: where chemistry and ML agree
text:
Locality: where chemistry and ML agree



Chemistry: a property is roughly a sum of group contributions
ML potential: the energy is a sum of contributions from each atom’s neighbourhood
Both say the whole is built from local parts


So compositional generalisation should come for free. Does it?





S. W. Benson, J. H. Buss, J. Chem. Phys. 29, 546 (1958); J. Behler, M. Parrinello, Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 146401 (2007).


This is the bridge between the two halves of the room: Benson’s additivity and the Behler–Parrinello energy decomposition have the same shape. Group-additivity values are schematic here.


How would we test that cleanly?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Our choice: scaffold out-of-distribution



Fusion: –OH and C=O seen apart; tested together on one carbon, as –COOH
Duplication: one –COOH seen; tested with two


Every group is in training; only the molecule is new.





A. M. Nourollah et al., NeurIPS (2026); arXiv:2605.08988.


Two examples now; the full set of five comes in the next section.


To run this test properly, we need a dataset built for it. That is GMD.

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
GMD: Generalisation for Molecular Dynamics



140 molecules in 12 families, built from H, C, N and O
300 K MD for each molecule, DFT energies and forces for every snapshot: about 280,000 configurations
Splits are by molecule, never by snapshot


Models are usually tested on new shapes of known molecules. GMD tests them on new molecules.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Open data and code: huggingface.co/datasets/AmirMasoud/GMD. Splitting by molecule is what makes this a test of new molecules rather than new frames.


“New molecule” can mean many things. Which kinds of novelty do we test?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Which kinds of compositionality?


Five aspects, from linguistics and ML
Systematicity, productivity, substitutivity, localism, overgeneralisation
GMD tests two of them
The two that transfer cleanly to atoms

Productivity
Handle longer structures than in training: one task, chain extension
Systematicity
Recombine known parts in new ways: four tasks, fusion, duplication, combination, fission


Each GMD task is one compositional operation, chosen from a framework the ML community already uses.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


For chemists: productivity is “bigger molecules from the same pieces”; systematicity is “new arrangements of the same pieces”. Substitutivity, localism and overgeneralisation do not transfer directly to atoms and are left to future work.


So what do these five operations look like?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Five ways to build a new molecule from known parts
text:
Five ways to build a new molecule from known parts







A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Abstract task on the left, real molecules on the right, row by row. Chain extension: C2–C6 alkanes in training, C7–C13 at test, motivated by drug discovery, where models trained on fragments must handle larger lead compounds. Fusion: C4–C10 with extra complex carbonyls and alcohols for coverage. Duplication and fission: C5–C10. Combination: C2–C9. Why small molecules: one operation per task, every part of a test molecule is in training, chemists can check the answers, and failing the smallest step is a strong result.


But if a model fails, is it because it never saw enough, or because it cannot compose?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Two reasons a model could fail
text:
Two reasons a model could fail


Missing coverage
The model never saw long chains, or never saw a group in a given setting
Fix: add the missing coverage to training

Missing composition
The model saw every piece, but never learned how pieces combine
Fix: show it a worked example of combining pieces


The augmented variants close the first gap and leave the second, so we can tell the two apart.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


What do the augmented variants look like?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
The augmented variants






Chain extension gets the missing coverage; fusion gets a worked example of composition.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Which models do we put through all of this?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Models and protocol


Trained from scratch
SchNet, DimeNet++, GemNet, PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, eSCN, EquiFormerV2: from the oldest to the newest designs, 2017 to 2024
Foundation models
MACE-MP-0 Small, Medium and Large and UMA-Small, fine-tuned per task; MACE-MP-0 Medium zero-shot

Error
Mean absolute error of energies and forces against DFT
ID and OOD
On known molecules (in-distribution) and new ones (out-of-distribution); headline: the OOD/ID ratio


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Foundation models fine-tuned for 2000 epochs per task: an upper bound on what fine-tuning can do. [Check seeds and error bars before the talk.]


So what happens on new molecules?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Known molecules versus new molecules






A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Each bar runs from a model’s error on known molecules (|) to its error on new ones, one marker per task; right column is the average OOD/ID ratio. MACE-Medium zero-shot shows ×1.0 only because it is already about ten times worse on known molecules. Energies are worse still: over 1000× on new molecules. In-distribution accuracy does not reliably predict out-of-distribution accuracy.


Where inside the molecule does the error appear?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Where the failure happens: inside the molecule
text:
Where the failure happens: inside the molecule



Hexanoic acid: new in the fusion task
Inner disc: error in force strength; ring: error in direction
Backbone fine; error on –COOH, mostly strength


Known: –OH and C=O. Not composed: –COOH.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Across tasks, direction errors localise on the heteroatoms of each task’s new environment: oxygen for fusion, duplication and fission; the O–N pairing for combination. The same atoms are fine where their environment matches training.


Combining parts fails badly. How does the simplest task, a longer chain, compare?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Chain extension: a smaller drop



Train on ethane to hexane; test on heptane to tridecane
Errors still rise with length, but far less than in the other four tasks
SchNet and DimeNet++ break down past the training lengths


Repeating a known part costs some accuracy. Combining parts in a new way costs far more.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


So is the problem coverage, or composition? The augmented variants answer that.

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
Coverage helps length, not composition


Augmented chain extension
Much easier for every model except SchNet: OOD/ID close to ×1, and DimeNet++ recovers
Coverage was the missing piece

Augmented fusion
The amide example does not help: errors on carboxylic acids stay as large as before
Composition is the missing piece


Consistent with models treating each group as a standalone token, not learning how groups combine.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Paper Figure 19 has the full results if you want to show them here.


And if we run fusion backwards, can a model split a group it only saw whole?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Fission: the group is learned as one unit
text:
Fission: the group is learned as one unit



Trained on carboxylic acids: –OH and C=O only ever appear together
Tested on alcohols and aldehydes: each part alone
The models cannot recover the parts


Consistent with –COOH being learned as one unit, not built up from its parts.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Related to localism in the compositionality framework, but not a direct test of it: the –OH and C=O environments in the test molecules differ physically from those inside –COOH.


Could bigger models, pre-training or a different level of theory close the gap?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Not a data, scale or label problem
text:
Not a data, scale or label problem


Pre-training
Foundation models pre-trained on millions of structures do not consistently beat MACE trained from scratch
Scale
Larger MACE-MP-0 helps on some tasks; the gap remains

Labels
GFN2-xTB labels instead of DFT give the same pattern
Coverage
Helps chain extension, not fusion (previous slides)


Fine-tuning fixes the molecules the model was shown, not the ones it was not.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


So what does all this mean, for chemists and for machine learning?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
text:
What it means


For chemists

Errors sit on the new functional group: wrong vibrations, conformers, barriers
They appear exactly where a molecule is new, which is where you would use a model
A good score on known molecules says little about yours


For machine learning

Locality in the architecture does not give compositional generalisation
Scale, pre-training and fine-tuning do not either
In-distribution accuracy does not reliably predict out-of-distribution accuracy



Before trusting a model on a new molecule, ask: has it seen this combination, or only these parts?


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


How far do these conclusions reach, and where should we look next?

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
section: Scope and next steps for the benchmark
text:
Scope and next steps for the benchmark


What GMD covers
Small H/C/N/O molecules in vacuum, one DFT level (PBE/def2-TZVP+D3BJ)
Why that is enough
Every part of each test molecule is in training: failure under this minimal shift is a strong result

What it does not cover
Aromatic, charged, inorganic or transition-metal chemistry; condensed phases
Natural extensions
Richer fragment vocabularies: peptides for proteins, monomers for polymers

So what do we take home, and can we teach a model to see molecules as we do?

What we found

More of the same (longer chains) costs some accuracy
Known parts in new combinations cost far more
Coverage, scale and pre-training do not fix composition
Models learn groups as units, not from their parts


What I am working on

A model whose learning is guided by chemical structure
Forcing it to see a molecule as a chemist does: functional groups and how they connect


Goal: a model that understands a new molecule from its parts.

High-energy geometries the data does not cover: one kind of out-of-distribution.





J. Behler, Chem. Rev. 121, 10037 (2021); X. Fu et al., Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (2023).


Schematic Morse-like curve. The tick marks along the bottom show where the MD samples fall.


Now think of a reaction. Which point on the path does MD visit least?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
section: Reactions: the rarest point matters most
text:
Reactions: the rarest point matters most



MD spends almost all its time in the reactant and product wells
The transition state is visited rarely, so it is barely in the data
At 298 K, every 1.4 kcal/mol of barrier error is a factor of 10 in the rate


Rare events the data barely covers: a second kind of out-of-distribution.





H. Eyring, J. Chem. Phys. 3, 107 (1935).


From k ∝ exp(−ΔG‡/RT): RT ln 10 ≈ 1.36 kcal/mol at 298 K. Schematic profile.


Steep walls, rare events… what else counts as out-of-distribution?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
Many ways to be out-of-distribution


Out-of-distribution: anything the training data does not represent, where the model has to go beyond its data rather than fill in between it.

High-energy geometries; rare events
Higher temperature than in training
Elements, charges or spin states never seen
Solvent or surfaces, when trained in vacuum
A new combination of known groups





S. Chmiela et al., Sci. Adv. 3, e1603015 (2017); X. Fu et al., Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (2023).


All but the last change the conditions. The last one changes only the composition: every part is covered, the whole is not.


That last one is the least tested. What would a test of it look like?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
Our choice: scaffold out-of-distribution



Fusion: –OH and C=O seen apart; tested together on one carbon, as –COOH
Duplication: one –COOH seen; tested with two


Every group is in training; only the molecule is new.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Two of the five GMD tasks, shown as examples; the full set comes in the next section. The question: does a model understand molecules the way we do, from their parts?


To run this test, we need a dataset built for it. That is GMD.

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
GMD: Generalisation for Molecular Dynamics



Carbon chains carrying –OH, –CHO, –COOH or –NH2
MD for each molecule, DFT energies and forces for every snapshot
Training and test sets contain different molecules, not just different snapshots


Usually models are tested on new shapes of known molecules. GMD tests them on new molecules.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Data and code are public: huggingface.co/datasets/AmirMasoud/GMD. Each molecule’s trajectory has about 2000 snapshots; 140 molecules in total.


So which new molecules do we test them on?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
section: Five ways to build a new molecule from known parts
text:
Five ways to build a new molecule from known parts







A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Walk down the rows: abstract task on the left, real molecules on the right. Why small molecules: each task changes exactly one thing, so a failure has one cause; every part of a test molecule is in training; chemists can check what a sensible answer looks like; failing the smallest possible step is a strong result.


So how do today’s models do?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
Known molecules versus new molecules






A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Each bar runs from a model’s error on known molecules (|) to its error on new ones, one marker per task; right column is the average OOD/ID ratio. MACE-Medium zero-shot shows ×1.0 only because it is already about ten times worse on known molecules. Energies are worse still: over 1000× on new molecules.


But where inside the molecule do these errors actually appear?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
section: Where the failure happens: inside the molecule
text:
Where the failure happens: inside the molecule



Hexanoic acid: new in the fusion task
Inner disc: error in force strength; ring: error in direction
Backbone fine; error on –COOH, mostly strength


–OH and C=O are known. –COOH is not.





A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Each atom’s error averaged over 200 test snapshots. NequIP spreads the error over the whole group; others concentrate it on one or two atoms. In the paper, directional errors also localise on the heteroatoms of each task’s new environment.


Combining parts fails badly. How does the simplest task, a longer chain, compare?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
Chain extension: a smaller drop



Train on ethane to hexane; test on heptane to tridecane
Errors still rise on longer chains, but far less than in the other four tasks
A longer chain adds more CH2, nothing chemically new


Repeating a known part costs some accuracy. Combining parts in a new way costs far more.





SchNet and DimeNet++ are the exceptions: their errors jump by orders of magnitude past hexane.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


So what do we take home from all this?

title: Knowing the parts, missing the whole: does machine learning understand new molecules built from what it already knows?
text:
Takeaways



More of the same (longer chains) costs some accuracy; known parts in new combinations cost far more
Wrong force strengths on a functional group mean wrong vibrations, wrong conformers, wrong barriers
More data, bigger models and pre-training do not fix it
Accuracy on known molecules does not predict accuracy on new ones





Before trusting a model on a new molecule, ask: has it seen this combination, or only these parts?


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.


Call back to the first slides: every molecule you care about is a new combination of familiar parts. Details on data and model size are in the appendix.

section: Not a data or model-size problem
text:
Not a data or model-size problem


More data
Foundation models pre-trained on millions of structures (MACE-MP-0, UMA) do not consistently beat MACE trained from scratch on GMD.
Bigger models
A larger MACE-MP-0 helps on some tasks, but the gap stays.

More training coverage
Adding related molecules to the training set does not close the gap for fusion.
Another level of theory
GFN2-xTB labels instead of DFT give the same pattern.


Fine-tuning fixes the molecules the model was shown, not the ones it wasn’t.


A. M. Nourollah, I. Khalid, S. Leoni, S. Schockaert, NeurIPS (2026), Evaluations & Datasets Track; arXiv:2605.08988.

A model whose learning is guided by chemical structure
It is forced to see a molecule the way a chemist does: as functional groups and how they connect

section: Fitting well is not generalising well
text:
Fitting well is not generalising well



Two kinds of points: the model learns a border between them
A straight line misses a few training points, but gets new points right
A wiggly border gets every training point right, and new points wrong


We want a model that works on data it has never seen, not one that remembers its training data. That is generalisation.





C. M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer (2006), §1.1, §4.1.


Point at the circled new points on the right panel. The over-fitted model “learned” the noise.


What about points that land outside everything the model has seen, or outside what our data covers?
